Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 53
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Painter
  trauma_type: Civilian in war zone
  pcl5: 34

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Smell): Related smells, Loss of Control: Lack of control, Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Meaning: go over and over why the event happened to me, Busyness: I work hard at keeping busy with other things, Avoid News: News reports about events similar to what happened to me
  Threat: Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Vignette:
Raj was 53, a painter living in a modest home in a quiet neighborhood, but the vibrant colors of his canvases belied the muted grays that now dominated his life. He had once found joy in his craft, expressing the beauty he saw around him, but that had changed after he had been caught in the crossfire of a civil conflict in his home country. The day of the explosion was etched in his memory, a chaotic blur of fire, smoke, and the desperate cries of others. He had narrowly escaped with his life, but the cost was immeasurable.

In the years following the incident, Raj found himself haunted by a mix of sensory triggers that ignited vivid flashbacks and anxiety. The faint whiff of diesel fuel, reminiscent of the trucks that had rumbled through his town the day of the explosion, would creep into his nostrils, sending him spiraling back to that moment of chaos. Even now, as he painted in his studio, the scent could drift in from the street, sending his heart racing and his hands trembling. He had come to believe that any smell could lead him back to that day, leaving him feeling utterly powerless.

His nights were filled with the echoes of explosions, the sharp cracks of gunfire ringing in his ears long after the sounds had faded. Ordinary noises—like the clatter of a dropped plate or the rumble of a car passing by—would make him jump as if a bomb were exploding beside him. He felt like a soldier on constant alert, every nerve ending tingling, as though danger lurked in every corner. His body was always on edge, tense and ready to react, as if he were still in the war zone he thought he had left behind.

To cope, Raj busied himself with work, pouring over his paintings in an attempt to drown out the memories. He painted from dawn until dusk, using every brushstroke to fend off the thoughts that relentlessly replayed the events of that day. He would ruminate on the “whys” of it all—why had this happened to him, why had he survived when so many others had not? The questions circled in his mind like vultures, and in the quiet moments, they clawed at him, deepening his sense of loss and grief. The world felt devoid of meaning; nothing seemed to matter anymore, not even his art, which had once been his lifeblood.

Raj had begun to avoid the news, knowing full well that any report of violence would only exacerbate his anxiety. The images and stories would pull him back into the memories he fought so hard to escape. He would turn off the television the moment he sensed a report on civil unrest, the mere thought of it sending a shiver down his spine. He felt isolated from the world, cut off from the connections he once cherished with friends and family. His wife, Aditi, tried to reach out, but he often found himself retreating, believing that he was a burden to her, that he was no longer the man she had married. The world, in his eyes, was a dangerous place, and he could not protect her from it.

As the months turned into years, Raj's life became a cycle of avoidance and grief. He no longer felt capable of the things that had once defined him, feeling as if he were merely a shadow of his former self. His paintings shifted from vibrant landscapes to dark and chaotic abstracts, reflecting the turmoil within him. Each brushstroke was a reminder of his lost potential, his lost joy, and the overwhelming sense of grief that accompanied every recollection of that fateful day.

It was during a particularly tense evening, as he sat in silence staring at an unfinished canvas, that the weight of his suffering suddenly felt unbearable. The thought crossed his mind that perhaps he needed help; perhaps this was more than he could manage alone. He had been avoiding his feelings, but now they loomed over him like a storm cloud, relentless and heavy. As he glanced at Aditi, who was gently urging him to share his thoughts, he realized that he feared the possibility of healing just as much as he feared remaining stuck in this cycle of pain. What terrified him most was the thought of opening up, of confronting the memories he had tried so hard to escape. But deep down, he also hoped for a way to reclaim the life he had lost, to find meaning and purpose again. With a deep breath, Raj knew that seeking help might be the first step towards rediscovering the colors of his world.
